claim: Each of the compound eyes is composed of approximately 800 units called ommatidia.
source: Each of the compound eyes is composed of approximately 800 units called ommatidia (Campos-Ortega, 1980)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Campos-Ortega, 1980.

claim: Each ommatidium contains eight photoreceptor or retinula cells (R1-R8).
source: each ommatidium contains eight photoreceptor or retinula cells (R1-R8)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ommatidial structure.

claim: Axons of R1-R6 photoreceptors terminate in the outermost lamina neuropile.
source: Axons of R1-R6 photoreceptors terminate in the outermost lamina neuropile (Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989.

claim: R8 and R7 axons project topographically through the lamina and terminate in the medulla.
source: In contrast, R8 and R7 axons project topographically through the lamina and terminate in the medulla (Figure 1 A).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A showing the projection pattern.

claim: R8 axons terminate in medulla layer M3.
source: Within the medulla column R8/R7 axons terminate in two different layers, M3 and M6 respectively (Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989.

claim: R7 axons terminate in medulla layer M6.
source: Within the medulla column R8/R7 axons terminate in two different layers, M3 and M6 respectively (Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989.

claim: R8/R7 axons contact their post-synaptic partner neurons in layers M3 and M6.
source: in which they contact their post-synaptic partner neurons (Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989; Gao et al., 2008; Karuppudurai et al., 2014; Melnattur and Lee, 2011; Ting et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: At 6 hr APF, 18 R8 axons innervate the medulla.
source: At 6 hr APF, 18 R8 (C arrowhead) and 15 R7 (C' arrowhead) axons innervate the medulla.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 1C and C''.

claim: At 6 hr APF, 15 R7 axons innervate the medulla.
source: At 6 hr APF, 18 R8 (C arrowhead) and 15 R7 (C' arrowhead) axons innervate the medulla.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 1C' and C''.

claim: At 12 hr APF, 24 R8 axons innervate the medulla.
source: At 12 hr APF, 24 R8 and 21 R7 axons innervate the medulla.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 1D and D''.

claim: At 12 hr APF, 21 R7 axons innervate the medulla.
source: At 12 hr APF, 24 R8 and 21 R7 axons innervate the medulla.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 1D' and D''.

claim: At 24 hr APF, 32 R8 axons have innervated the medulla field.
source: At 24 hr APF, 32 R8 and 29 R7 axons have innervated the medulla field.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 1E and E''.

claim: At 24 hr APF, 29 R7 axons have innervated the medulla field.
source: At 24 hr APF, 32 R8 and 29 R7 axons have innervated the medulla field.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 1E' and E''.

claim: R cell axon innervation in the medulla mirrors the temporal pattern of R cell specification.
source: we could show that R cell axon innervation in the medulla mirrors the temporal pattern of R cell specification and follows a consistent sequence of growth cone segregation for each stage
evidence: The claim is supported by the quantification data from multiple developmental stages shown in Figure 1C-E''.

claim: The first R7 axon arrives about 6 hr after the youngest R8 axon and three columns posterior to it.
source: followed by the arrival of the first R7 axon at the respective R8 position about 6 hr later and three columns posterior to the youngest R8 axon (Figure 1C' arrowhead).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 1C'.

claim: R7/R8 growth cones are in close contact for 6-8 hr, represented by 3-4 columns.
source: For the next 6-8 hr, represented by 3–4 columns, R7/R8 growth cones are in close contact followed by their segregation into adjacent positions
evidence: The claim is based on temporal and spatial analysis of growth cone positions.

claim: R7 growth cones locate proximal with respect to the superficial R8 growth cones in the corresponding columns.
source: with R7 growth cones locating proximal with respect to the superficial R8 growth cones in the corresponding columns ('R7-R8 segregation', Figure 1C'-E').
evidence: The claim is supported by images in Figure 1C'-E'.

claim: Sequoia is critical for R cell target layer selection.
source: As reported previously, Sequoia is critical for R cell target layer selection (Petrovic and Hummel, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Petrovic and Hummel, 2008.

claim: Axons of sequoia mutant R8 cells project to the anterior medulla in the wild type sequence.
source: Axons of sequoia mutant R8 cells project to the anterior medulla in the wild type sequence but convergence of neighbouring R8 growth cones can be observed, disrupting the topographic organization (Figure 2A–B').
evidence: The claim is supported by MARCM analysis shown in Figure 2A-B'.

claim: Sequoia mutant R8 growth cones converge upon arrival at the anterior medulla, disrupting topographic organization.
source: Axons of sequoia mutant R8 cells project to the anterior medulla in the wild type sequence but convergence of neighbouring R8 growth cones can be observed, disrupting the topographic organization (Figure 2A–B').
evidence: The claim is supported by MARCM analysis shown in Figure 2B'.

claim: Sequoia mutant R7 growth cones fail to segregate from R8 growth cones at 6 hr APF.
source: Similar to R8, no defects can be detected in the extension and arrival of sequoia mutant R7 axons but they fail to segregate from R8 growth cones within the same column as early as 6 hr APF (Figure 2C–D').
evidence: The claim is supported by MARCM analysis shown in Figure 2D'.

claim: Sequoia mutant R7 growth cones remain at the superficial medulla position together with R8 growth cones at 24 hr APF.
source: Subsequently, these sequoia mutant R7 growth cones remain at the superficial medulla position together with R8 growth cones even at 24 hr APF (Figure 2E–F').
evidence: The claim is supported by MARCM analysis shown in Figure 2F'.

claim: Sequoia mutant R7 growth cones from two neighbouring columns converge in the superficial medulla position.
source: Interestingly, sequoia mutant R7 growth cones from two neighbouring columns also converge in the superficial medulla position (Figure 2G–G').
evidence: The claim is supported by MARCM analysis shown in Figure 2G'.

claim: Sequoia has a cell-autonomous function in growth cone segregation.
source: Single cell analysis revealed a cell-autonomous function of Sequoia in growth cone segregation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B', arrowhead).
evidence: The claim is supported by single cell MARCM analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of Sequoia function disrupts the sequential segregation of R8-R8, R8-R7 and R7-R7 growth cones within as well as between layers.
source: Therefore, loss of Sequoia function disrupts the sequential segregation of R8-R8, R8-R7 and R7-R7 growth cones within as well as between layers.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined loss-of-function data for R8 and R7 cells.

claim: In wild type R8 background, sequoia mutant R7 from the same ommatidium will terminate together in M3.
source: In case of wild type R8 axons, sequoia mutant R7 from the same ommatidium will terminate together in M3 (Figure 2I,I')
evidence: The claim is supported by MARCM analysis shown in Figure 2I'.

claim: A sequoia mutant R8 and R7 co-terminate in M1.
source: whereas a sequoia mutant R8 and R7 co-terminate in M1 (Petrovic and Hummel, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Petrovic and Hummel, 2008.

claim: Wild type R7 growth cones segregate from ectopic R8 growth cones and reach layer M6 when R8 axons are retained in layer M1 via Golden-goal over-expression.
source: Wild type R7 growth cones segregate from ectopic R8 growth cones and reach the layer M6 (Figure 2J–J'), indicating that the ectopic position of R8 axons does not influence wild type R7 axon targeting.
evidence: The claim is supported by MARCM analysis in GMR-gogo background shown in Figure 2J'.

claim: Sequoia mutant R7 axons mis-target to layer M1 along with ectopic R8 axons when R8 is retained in M1 via GMR-gogo.
source: In contrast, sequoia mutant R7 axons mis-target to layer M1 along with ectopic R8 axons (Figure 2K–K').
evidence: The claim is supported by MARCM analysis in GMR-gogo background shown in Figure 2K'.

claim: Mis-targeting of sequoia mutant R7 axons is the consequence of growth cone segregation defects rather than a change in target layer recognition.
source: This indicates that mis-targeting of sequoia mutant R7 axons is the consequence of growth cone segregation defects rather than a change in target layer recognition.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the GMR-gogo experiments showing that sequoia mutant R7 follows R8 position.

claim: Sequoia regulates point-to-point spacing of axons of the same R cell type within the temporary layer.
source: For axons of the same R cell type but from different ommatidia, Sequoia supports point-to-point spacing within the temporary layer and thereby controls the subsequent columnar restriction.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the R8-R8 and R7-R7 convergence phenotypes in sequoia mutants.

claim: Sequoia mediates the segregation of R7/R8 growth cones between layers for cells from a single ommatidium.
source: In addition, for the pair of R7/R8 cells from a single ommatidium, which innervate the same medulla column, Sequoia mediates the segregation of growth cones between layers.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the R7-R8 segregation defects in sequoia mutants.

claim: Sequoia shows a highly restricted expression during early differentiation of all R cells.
source: Sequoia shows a highly restricted expression during early differentiation of all R cells (Petrovic and Hummel, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Petrovic and Hummel, 2008.

claim: A short peak of high Sequoia expression at the onset of R cell differentiation is followed by a rapid decline in protein levels.
source: A short peak of high Sequoia expression at the onset of R cell differentiation is followed by a rapid decline in protein levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A graph).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The short peak of Sequoia expression in each cell leads to small differences of Sequoia levels in sequentially projecting R8 cells from adjacent ommatidial rows.
source: Due to the sequential development of ommatidia in the eye field as well as R cell types within each ommatidium (Tomlinson and Ready, 1987), the short peak of Sequoia expression in each cell leads to small differences of Sequoia levels in sequentially projecting R8 cells from adjacent ommatidial rows ('inter-ommatidial differences', Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Figure 3K1a).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the temporal dynamics of Sequoia expression and sequential R cell development.

claim: Each R7 develops approximately 8 hr after R8 in every ommatidium corresponding to four ommatidial rows in the eye disc.
source: In addition, each R7 develops approximately 8 hr after R8 in every ommatidium corresponding to four ommatidial rows in the eye disc.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of R cell development timing.

claim: The highest difference in Sequoia expression levels is found between R8 and R7 cells of the same ommatidium with almost no detectable Sequoia in R8 at the time of maximal Sequoia expression in R7.
source: Therefore, the highest difference in the expression levels of Sequoia can be found between these two cell types with almost no detectable Sequoia in R8 at the time of maximal Sequoia expression in the R7 of the same ommatidium ('intra-ommatidial differences', Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, inset 3, Figure 3K1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by Sequoia expression analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Prolonged Sequoia expression using LGMR-Gal4 leads to convergence of R7/R8 growth cones in the deeper medulla position.
source: Abolishing the inter-ommatidial differences via prolonged Sequoia expression using LGMR-Gal4 leads to a convergence of R7/R8 growth cones in the deeper medulla position (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B').
evidence: The claim is supported by gain-of-function analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B'.

claim: Equalizing Sequoia levels in only R7 cells using sev-Gal4 results in frequent R7 growth cone convergence and corresponding innervation gaps in the deeper medulla layer.
source: Similarly, equalizing Sequoia levels in only R7 cells using sev-Gal4, which shows transient, low-level expression as compared to LGMR-Gal4, resulted in frequent R7 growth cone convergence and corresponding innervation gaps in the deeper medulla layer (Figure 3A–B', arrowheads in B').
evidence: The claim is supported by gain-of-function analysis shown in Figure 3B'.

claim: Loss and gain of Sequoia activity lead to similar growth cone convergence phenotypes.
source: This result shows that the loss and gain of Sequoia activity leads to similar growth cone convergence phenotypes indicating that the presence of Sequoia expression is not sufficient to mediate growth cone segregation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing loss-of-function and gain-of-function phenotypes.

claim: The majority of single Seqhigh R7 axons segregate from the surrounding wild type Seqlow axons and project deeper into the medulla.
source: Here we observed that the majority of single Seqhigh R7 axons segregate from the surrounding wild type Seqlow axons and project deeper into the medulla (Figure 3D').
evidence: The claim is supported by mosaic analysis shown in Figure 3D'.

claim: Most mosaics with two adjacent Seqhigh R7 cells show growth cone convergence and termination at the appropriate medulla position.
source: In contrast to the single cell clones, most of the mosaics with two adjacent Seqhigh R7 cells show growth cone convergence and termination at the appropriate medulla position (Figure 3D").
evidence: The claim is supported by mosaic analysis shown in Figure 3D".

claim: Single Seqhigh R7 cells from distant columns often converge in the inner medulla neuropile or within the lobula complex.
source: Interestingly, single Seqhigh R7 cells from distant columns, which overshoot the temporary layer, often converge in the inner medulla neuropile (Figure 3D' arrow) or even within the lobula complex (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by mosaic analysis shown in Figure 3D'.

claim: Single Seqhigh R8 axons segregate from the surrounding wild type Seqlow R8 axons and extend further into the medulla neuropile.
source: Similar to R7, mosaics of R8 cells with different Sequoia expression levels segregate during initial axon positioning: single Seqhigh R8 axons segregate from the surrounding wild type Seqlow R8 axons (Figure 3E' arrowhead) and extend further into the medulla neuropile (Figure 3E' arrow)
evidence: The claim is supported by mosaic analysis shown in Figure 3E'.

claim: Two or more neighbouring Seqhigh R8 growth cones converge and terminate at the R7 position.
source: whereas two or more neighbouring Seqhigh R8 growth cones converge and terminate at the R7 position (Figure 3E" arrow).
evidence: The claim is supported by mosaic analysis shown in Figure 3E".

claim: Equalized Sequoia levels prevent growth cone segregation.
source: Thus, together with the loss-of-function, this gain-of-function analyses show that 'equalized' Sequoia levels prevent growth cone segregation thereby highlighting the role of relative Sequoia levels in this process (summarized in Figure 3K2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from combined loss-of-function and gain-of-function analyses.

claim: Sequoia mutant R1-6 growth cones fail to segregate normally, illustrated by gaps within the lamina plexus.
source: The sequoia mutant R1-6 growth cones fail to segregate normally, illustrated by gaps within the lamina plexus (Figure 3H–H", Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-E')
evidence: The claim is supported by MARCM analysis shown in Figure 3H" and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E'.

claim: Clones of Seqhigh R1-6 cells segregate their growth cones from the wild type ones thereby organizing the formation of a novel layer within the lamina neuropile.
source: Strikingly, clones of Seqhigh R1-6 cells segregate their growth cones from the wild type (Seqlow) ones thereby organizing the formation of a novel layer within the lamina neuropile (Figure 3I–J", Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,F').
evidence: The claim is supported by mosaic analysis shown in Figure 3J" and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F'.

claim: Large differences in Sequoia levels among R cells segregate their growth cones into distinct layers.
source: This demonstrates that large differences in Sequoia levels among R cells, either inherently present as in case of developing R7/R8 cells or ectopically generated as in case of R1-R6 cells, segregate their growth cones into distinct layers.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the R7/R8 and R1-6 gain-of-function analyses.

claim: Cells with higher Sequoia levels position their growth cones deeper in the neuropile.
source: In all cases, cells with higher Sequoia levels position their growth cones deeper in the neuropile.
evidence: The claim is inferred from all the gain-of-function experiments showing deeper positioning with higher Sequoia.

claim: Small differences in Sequoia levels lead to evenly-spaced growth cone positioning within a layer.
source: From these data we propose a 'Growth Cone Segregation' model, in which small differences in Sequoia levels lead to an evenly–spaced growth cone positioning within a layer
evidence: The claim is a model proposed based on the experimental data.

claim: Large Sequoia differences result in segregation of growth cones into separate layers.
source: whereas large Sequoia differences result in segregation of growth cones into separate layers.
evidence: The claim is a model proposed based on the experimental data.

claim: Equal levels of Sequoia in projecting R cells cause the convergence of growth cones and termination of axonal extension.
source: In contrast, equal levels of Sequoia in projecting R cells, either in loss- or gain-of-function context, cause the convergence of growth cones and termination of axonal extension (Figure 3K).
evidence: The claim is a model proposed based on the experimental data.

claim: An R8 growth cone shift to deeper medulla position can be observed following Sequoia expression until 24 hr APF.
source: Using this method, an R8 growth cone shift to deeper medulla position can be observed following Sequoia expression until 24 hr APF (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal control experiments using Gal80ts shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: An onset of Sequoia expression after 24 hr APF has no effect on R7/R8 growth cone segregation.
source: In contrast, an onset of Sequoia expression after 24 hr APF, at which time all photoreceptor axons have arrived in the target field, has no effect on R7/ R8 growth cone segregation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal control experiments using Gal80ts shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: R7/R8 cells are sensitive to Sequoia-induced growth cone segregation only during a narrow developmental window.
source: This indicates that R7/R8 cells are sensitive to Sequoia-induced growth cone segregation only during a narrow developmental window.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the temporal control experiments showing no effect after 24 hr APF.

claim: R8 growth cones respond to elevated Sequoia levels after 24 hr APF by leaving their topographic position and converging onto neighbouring growth cones.
source: Interestingly, although R8 growth cones do not change the layer upon Sequoia expression after 24 hr APF, they still respond to these elevated Sequoia levels by leaving their topographic position and converging onto neighbouring growth cones (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal control experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The restriction of R cell growth cones to distinct temporary layers occurs immediately following their segregation.
source: This indicates that the restriction of R cell growth cones to distinct temporary layers occurs immediately following their segregation
evidence: The claim is inferred from the temporal sensitivity experiments.

claim: The process of columnar restriction continues into the later steps of visual map formation.
source: whereas the process of columnar restriction continues into the later steps of visual map formation (Ferguson et al., 2009; Ting et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and inferred from the late Sequoia expression effects on topography.

claim: Upon induction of Sequoia expression at 6 hr APF, the youngest 10 R8 growth cones shift to the deeper R7 position whereas the more posterior 8 R8 growth cones remain at their superficial medulla position.
source: Upon the induction of Sequoia expression at 6 hr APF with about 18 R8 growth cones in the medulla target region, we observed a defined shift of the youngest 10 of these R8 growth cones to the deeper R7 position whereas the more posterior, and therefore older, 8 R8 growth cones remain at their superficial medulla position.
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal pulse experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: At 8 hr APF, 12 out of 20 R8 growth cones are no longer responsive to elevated Sequoia levels.
source: Two hours later (at 8 hr APF), four more R8 growth cones (12 out of 20) are no longer responsive to elevated Sequoia levels as they do not leave their superficial medulla positions (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal pulse experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Upon the onset of Sequoia expression at 12 hr APF, 16 out of 24 R8 growth cones are retained in the superficial medulla position.
source: Upon the onset of Sequoia expression at 12 hr APF, 16 out of 24 R8 growth cones are retained in the superficial medulla position (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal pulse experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Continuous Sequoia expression at later developmental stages does not disrupt the superficial layer positioning of R8 growth cones that are consolidated prior to Sequoia induction.
source: Additionally, continuous Sequoia expression at later developmental stages does not disrupt the superficial layer positioning of R8 growth cones that are consolidated prior to Sequoia induction (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal pulse experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The consolidation of each R8 growth cone occurs approximately 18 hr after its arrival at the superficial medulla layer.
source: Together, the consolidation of each R8 growth cone occurs approximately 18 hr after its arrival at the superficial medulla layer (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the temporal pulse experiments and quantified in Figure 4F.

claim: For each R8 growth cone there is a defined transition from the initial positioning to the consolidation shortly after R7-R8 segregation.
source: The fixed correlation between the number of consolidated R8 growth cones and developmental time indicates that for each R8 growth cone there is a defined transition from the initial positioning to the consolidation shortly after R7-R8 segregation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the temporal pulse experiments.

claim: Capricious is expressed in projecting R8 cells.
source: Capricious (Caps) is expressed in projecting R8 cells and has been proposed to mediate R8 axon targeting (Shinza-Kameda et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shinza-Kameda et al., 2006.

claim: At the anterior medulla, Capricious shows a homogeneous expression with NFI ratios for R cell growth cones and corresponding medulla region being close to 1.
source: At the anterior medulla, Capricious shows a homogeneous expression with NFI ratios for R cell growth cones and corresponding medulla region being close to 1 (0.94 in R8 and 0.87 in R7 growth cone position, Figure 5A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Capricious expression shown in Figure 5 and the table.

claim: Following the phase of growth cone segregation, Capricious enriches during the process of consolidation at the region of R8 growth cones with an NFI ratio increasing to 1.39.
source: Following the phase of growth cone segregation, Capricious enriches during the process of consolidation at the region of R8 growth cones with an NFI ratio increasing to 1.39 and a four fold decline at the R7 position (with the ratio of 0.24, Figure 5A'–D').
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of Capricious expression shown in Figure 5A'-D' and the table.

claim: During the process of consolidation, Capricious levels in R8 growth cones increase.
source: This indicates that during the process of consolidation, Capricious levels in R8 growth cones increase.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the Capricious expression quantification.

claim: Capricious-negative R7 growth cones move to a deeper medulla position devoid of any Capricious expression.
source: At the same time, Capricious-negative R7 growth cones move to a deeper medulla position devoid of any Capricious expression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the Capricious expression pattern showing decline at R7 position.

claim: No defect could be detected in the initial position of capricious mutant R8 growth cones as well as subsequent R7/R8 segregation.
source: Interestingly, no defect could be detected in the initial position of R8 growth cones as well as subsequent R7/R8 segregation (Figure 5E–E",G,G').
evidence: The claim is supported by MARCM analysis of capricious mutants shown in Figure 5G'.

claim: R8 growth cone positioning defects in capricious mutants first appear during the phase of consolidation where capricious mutant growth cones extend towards the deeper R7 position.
source: R8 growth cone positioning defects first appear during the phase of consolidation where capricious mutant growth cones extend towards the deeper R7 position (Figure 5G").
evidence: The claim is supported by MARCM analysis shown in Figure 5G".

claim: Capricious mutant R8 axons mis-target to layer M6.
source: Later in development, these capricious mutant R8 axons mis-target to layer M6 as previously reported (Figure 5F–H", Shinza-Kameda et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by MARCM analysis shown in Figure 5H" and citation.

claim: Capricious is not required for the initial positioning of R8 growth cones and R7/R8 segregation but is critical for the subsequent step of R8 growth cone consolidation in the superficial medulla.
source: This shows that Capricious is not required for the initial positioning of R8 growth cones and R7/R8 segregation but is critical for the subsequent step of R8 growth cone consolidation in the superficial medulla.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the temporal analysis of capricious mutant phenotypes.

claim: Partial reduction of Capricious levels via targeted RNAi does not interfere with the consolidation of R8 growth cones in the superficial medulla position.
source: The partial reduction of Capricious levels via targeted RNAi does not interfere with the consolidation of R8 growth cones in the superficial medulla position (Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 5I.

claim: RNAi-mediated Capricious reduction in the background of elevated Sequoia expression severely affected the R8 growth cone consolidation resulting in most of the posterior R8 growth cones shifting to the deeper R7 position.
source: In contrast, the RNAi-mediated Capricious reduction in the background of elevated Sequoia expression severely affected the R8 growth cone consolidation resulting in most of the posterior R8 growth cones shifting to the deeper R7 position (Figure 5K,L).
evidence: The claim is supported by combined RNAi and Sequoia expression experiments shown in Figure 5K,L.

claim: Co-expression of Sequoia and Capricious prevents Sequoia-induced shift of R8 growth cones and leads to segregation of R7 and R8 growth cones in a wild type pattern.
source: Furthermore, co-expression of Sequoia and Capricious prevents Sequoia-induced shift of R8 growth cones and leads to segregation of R7 and R8 growth cones in a wild type pattern (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B').
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B'.

claim: Sequoia mediated growth cone segregation and Capricious mediated adhesion are antagonistic forces that are capable of balancing each other to achieve proper positioning of R-cell growth cones in the developing medulla.
source: Therefore, Sequoia mediated growth cone segregation and Capricious mediated adhesion are antagonistic forces that are capable of balancing each other to achieve proper positioning of R-cell growth cones in the developing medulla.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined Sequoia and Capricious manipulation experiments.

claim: All R7 and R8 axons simultaneously extend during the second half of medulla circuit assembly to the M6 and M3 layer respectively.
source: Following the sequential positioning of R7/R8 growth cones during the first half of pupal development, all R7 and R8 axons simultaneously extend during the second half of medulla circuit assembly to the M6 and M3 layer respectively (Ting and Lee, 2007; Özel et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ting and Lee, 2007 and Özel et al., 2015.

claim: A pulse of Sequoia expression until 24 hr APF leads to an initial shift of all R8 growth cones to the deeper R7 position.
source: A pulse of Sequoia expression until 24 hr APF and subsequent repression using Gal80ts leads to an initial shift of all R8 growth cones to the deeper R7 position (Figure 6C,C').
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal control experiments shown in Figure 6C'.

claim: R8 axons initially shifted to deeper R7 position by Sequoia pulse terminate in layer M6 together with R7 axons even without further Sequoia expression.
source: Interestingly, in the subsequent steps of synaptic layer targeting, these R8 axons, together with R7 axons, terminate in the layer M6 even without further Sequoia expression (Figure 6D,D').
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal control experiments shown in Figure 6D'.

claim: An early Sequoia pulse until 6 hr APF leads to a shift of 8-10 posterior R8 growth cones towards the deeper R7 medulla position.
source: Additionally, an early Sequoia pulse until 6 hr APF leads to a shift of 8–10 posterior R8 growth cones towards the deeper R7 medulla position (Figure 6E,E').
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal control experiments shown in Figure 6E'.

claim: R8 axons recognize their final target layer exactly according to their initial growth cone position.
source: Following this pattern during the subsequent steps of medulla development reveals that R8 axons recognize their final target layer exactly according to their initial growth cone position (Figure 6F,F')
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal control experiments shown in Figure 6F'.

claim: No difference in Capricious and Frazzled expression can be detected in R8 cells with elevated Sequoia levels.
source: However, no difference in Capricious and Frazzled expression can be detected in R8 cells with elevated Sequoia levels (Figure 6G-J')
evidence: The claim is supported by expression analysis shown in Figure 6G-J'.

claim: Sequoia does not influence cell-type specific differentiation programs of R7 and R8.
source: which is in line with earlier data showing that Sequoia does not influence cell-type specific differentiation programs of R7 and R8 (Petrovic and Hummel, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Petrovic and Hummel, 2008.

claim: Dm8 neurites and mis-positioned R8 growth cones are in close proximity.
source: Therefore the Dm8 neurites and mis-positioned R8 growth cones are also in close proximity raising the possibility that these two cell types can directly interact with each other (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–B').
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-B'.

claim: In wild type, R7 axons form GRASP-positive connections with Dm8 in layer M6.
source: In wild type (Figure 6K–K"), the expression of pre-synaptic syb::spGFP1-10 in R7/R8 (LGMR-Gal4) and post-synaptic LexAop-spGFP11::CD4, in Dm8 cells (OrtC1-3 LexA DBD, OrtC2B dVP16AD; Karuppudurai et al., 2014; See Materials and methods for details), results in GRASP-positive R7->Dm8 connections in layer M6 (Figure 6K" arrows)
evidence: The claim is supported by syb-GRASP experiments shown in Figure 6K".

claim: No GRASP-positive R8->Dm8 connections can be detected in layer M3 in wild type.
source: and no GRASP-positive R8->Dm8 connections can be detected in layer M3 (Figure 6K" arrowheads).
evidence: The claim is supported by syb-GRASP experiments shown in Figure 6K".

claim: When R7 growth cones are retained at the R8 temporary layer via UAS-CapriciousID expression, GRASP signal demonstrating R7->Dm8 contacts can be observed only in columns where escaper R7 axons target to layer M6.
source: When R7 growth cones are retained at the R8 temporary layer via UAS-CapriciousID expression using sev-Gal4 (Shinza-Kameda et al., 2006), GRASP signal, demonstrating R7->Dm8 contacts, can be observed only in columns where 'escaper' R7 axons target to layer M6 (Figure 6L" arrows), but not in columns with mis-targeted R7 axons (Figure 6L" arrowhead).
evidence: The claim is supported by syb-GRASP experiments with CapriciousID shown in Figure 6L".

claim: GRASP-positive R8->Dm8 connections can be detected in medulla layer M6 following the early shift of R8 growth cones to the deeper medulla position.
source: Surprisingly, GRASP-positive R8->Dm8, similar to R7->Dm8, connections can be detected in medulla layer M6 following the early shift of R8 growth cones to the deeper medulla position (Figure 6M–M")
evidence: The claim is supported by syb-GRASP experiments with Sequoia expression shown in Figure 6M".

claim: Both R7 and R8 can recognize Dm8 processes and form synaptic contacts.
source: indicating that both R7 and R8 can recognize Dm8 processes and form synaptic contacts.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the syb-GRASP experiments showing R8->Dm8 contacts when R8 is mis-positioned.

claim: Early, birth order dependent, segregation of R cell growth cones determines later synaptic layer identity in the Drosophila visual system.
source: Here we demonstrate that the early, birth order dependent, segregation of R cell growth cones determines later synaptic layer identity in the Drosophila visual system.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claim: Small inter-ommatidial differences in Sequoia levels organize R cell growth cones within a layer.
source: Small inter-ommatidial differences in Sequoia levels organize R cell growth cones within a layer
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the Sequoia expression and functional analyses.

claim: Large intra-ommatidial differences in Sequoia levels segregate growth cones between layers.
source: whereas large intra-ommatidial differences segregate growth cones between layers.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the Sequoia expression and functional analyses.

claim: Changes in the positioning of growth cones directly correlate with changes in synaptic layer selection without affecting the expression of known cell-type specific targeting molecules.
source: Changes in the positioning of growth cones directly correlate with changes in synaptic layer selection without affecting the expression of known cell-type specific targeting molecules.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the temporal control experiments and expression analyses.

claim: Initial afferent growth cone positioning is an essential pre-requisite for visual map formation prior to synaptic partner recognition.
source: These results highlight the importance of initial afferent growth cone positioning for visual map formation prior to synaptic partner recognition (Figure 7).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: An early shift in the R8 growth cones to R7 position allows them to recognize the R7 target cell Dm8 as synaptic partner later during development.
source: An early shift in the R8 growth cones to R7 position, induced by a short pulse of Sequoia expression, allows them to recognize the R7 target cell Dm8 as synaptic partner later during the development.
evidence: This is a summary of the Sequoia pulse and GRASP experiments.

claim: If R7 growth cones fail to segregate from R8 growth cones, they terminate together with R8 axons in the M3 synaptic layer independent of their intrinsic differentiation and targeting program.
source: Similarly, if R7 growth cones fail to segregate from R8 growth cones, they terminate together with R8 axons in the M3 synaptic layer independent of their intrinsic differentiation and targeting program.
evidence: This is a summary of the sequoia mutant R7 phenotypes.

claim: Expression of LAR as membrane tethered ligand in R8 cells alone could induce a response from R7 axons, indicating direct signalling between R8-R7 axons.
source: Support for direct interaction between R7-R8 afferents comes from Maurel-Zaffran et al., 2001, where the expression of LAR as membrane tethered ligand in R8 cells alone (using an R8-specific Gal4 driver line) could induce a response from R7 axons, indicating a direct signalling between R8-R7 axons.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maurel-Zaffran et al., 2001.

claim: Induced Capricious expression in R8 and R7 cells in Capricious null background is sufficient to mis-target R7 axons to layer M3, indicating direct R7-R8 afferent interaction.
source: Further, induced Capricious expression in R8 and R7 cells, in Capricious null background (therefore resulting in a target region without any Capricious expression) is sufficient to mis-target R7 axons to layer M3, again indicating a direct R7-R8 afferent interaction (Berger-Müller et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Berger-Müller et al., 2013.

claim: Final target layer of sequoia mutant R7 axons depends on the targeting of R8 axons.
source: Here we show that final target layer of sequoia mutant R7 axons depends on the targeting of R8 axons, further suggesting that mis-targeting of sequoia mutant R7 axons to ectopic synaptic layer is the consequence of segregation defect rather than a change in target layer recognition.
evidence: This is a summary of the GMR-gogo experiments with sequoia mutants.

claim: Relative levels of Sequoia determine the segregation of afferent R7/R8 growth cones within or between layers.
source: Here we show that in the Drosophila visual system, relative levels of Sequoia determine the segregation of afferent R7/R8 growth cones within or between layers.
evidence: This is a summary of the Sequoia expression and functional analyses.

claim: Endogenous differences in Sequoia levels most likely arise as a result of the temporal sequence of R cell specification, suggesting a self-patterning mechanism in early visual circuit assembly.
source: The endogenous differences in Sequoia levels most likely arise as a result of the temporal sequence of R cell specification, suggesting a self-patterning mechanism in early visual circuit assembly (Hassan and Hiesinger, 2015; Roignant and Treisman, 2009, Tomlinson and Ready, 1987).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the Sequoia expression dynamics and supported by citations.

claim: Capricious mediated growth cone consolidation removes the temporal difference in the arrival of R8 axons.
source: We speculate that Capricious mediated growth cone consolidation serves two purposes: 1. It removes the temporal difference in the arrival of R8 axons
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the Capricious functional data.

claim: Capricious mediated growth cone consolidation maintains R8 axons in the position where they are responsive to subsequent NetrinB signal provided by L3 neurites.
source: and 2. It maintains R8 axons in the position where they are responsive to subsequent NetrinB signal provided by L3 neurites (Pecot et al., 2014; Timofeev et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the Capricious functional data and supported by citations.

claim: Displacement of R8 growth cones to deeper medulla position leads to their mis-targeting to layer M6 in spite of normal Frazzled expression.
source: First, as we show in this study, the displacement of R8 growth cones to deeper medulla position leads to their mis-targeting to layer M6 in spite of normal Frazzled expression in these R8 cells.
evidence: This is a summary of the Sequoia pulse experiments and Frazzled expression analysis.

claim: Ectopic expression of Frazzled in R7 cells cannot re-direct them to M3 layer in response to localized NetrinB signal.
source: Second, the ectopic expression of Frazzled in R7 cells cannot re-direct them to M3 layer in response to localized NetrinB signal present in the superficial position
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: R8 axons can be re-directed to a different layer (M1/M2) by ectopic expression of localized NetrinB in a position deeper to the superficial R8 medulla position.
source: but R8 axons can be re-directed to a different layer (M1/M2) by ectopic expression of localized NetrinB in a position deeper to the superficial R8 medulla position (Nern et al., 2008; Pecot et al., 2013; Timofeev et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: M3 layer targeting via L3-mediated NetrinB signalling requires R8 axons to be positioned superficially in the medulla.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that M3 layer targeting via L3-mediated NetrinB signalling requires R8 axons to be positioned superficially in the medulla further underscoring the importance of R8 growth cone consolidation in this position (Figure 7).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on R8 positioning and NetrinB signalling.

claim: R7 growth cones are in close proximity with their primary post-synaptic target neurons, Dm8, at the end of growth cone segregation.
source: We confirm previous observations, that R7 growth cones are in close proximity with their primary post-synaptic target neurons, Dm8, at the end of growth cone segregation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B', Ting et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data and citation to Ting et al., 2014.

claim: Targeting of R7 axons to M6 layer could be the direct result of R7->Dm8 contacts mediated by N-Cadherin.
source: This raises the possibility that targeting of R7 axons to M6 layer, later in the development, could be the direct result of R7->Dm8 contacts mediated by N-Cadherin.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the proximity data and N-Cadherin function.

claim: N-Cadherin function is necessary for stabilizing R7 growth cones in the deeper medulla position.
source: Recently it was shown that N-Cadherin function is necessary for stabilizing R7 growth cones in the deeper medulla position but not for targeting and subsequent extension of R7 axons to M6 layer seems to be a result of passive dislocation (Özel et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Özel et al., 2015.

claim: Early expression of Sequoia in CadN mutant R7 cells can rescue the mis-targeting of R7 growth cones in the superficial medulla position at 24 hr APF but fails to rescue the later mis-targeting to layer M3.
source: Additional support for the role of N-Cadherin in the formation and maintenance of R7->Dm8 contacts, following their initial segregation from R8 growth cones, comes from our observation that early expression of Sequoia in CadN mutant R7 cells under weak elav-Gal4 driver can rescue the mis-targeting of R7 growth cones in the superficial medulla position along with R8 growth cones at 24 hr APF (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,A',C,C'), but fails to rescue the later mis-targeting to layer M3 eventually resulting in a mis-targeting phenotype identical to CadN mutant R7 axons (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B,B',D,D').
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: R8 growth cones initially mis-positioned in the deeper medulla eventually mis-target to layer M6 and form synaptic contacts with Dm8.
source: Interestingly, the R8 growth cones initially mis-positioned in the deeper medulla eventually mis-target to layer M6 and form synaptic contacts with Dm8.
evidence: This is a summary of the Sequoia pulse and GRASP experiments.

claim: R8 cells with axons mis-targeted to layer M6 do not show changes in any of their known cell-type specific molecules including Senseless, Frazzled, Capricious and Rh6.
source: In addition, these R8 cells, with axons mis-targeted to layer M6, do not show changes in any of their known cell-type specific molecules including early specifier of cell identity (Senseless), guidance receptors (Frazzled, Capricious) and sensory receptors (Rh6).
evidence: This is a summary of the expression analyses in mis-positioned R8 cells.

claim: No expression of R7 specific molecules (Prospero, R3, Rh4) can be detected in R8 cells with axons mis-targeted to M6.
source: In addition, no expression of R7 specific molecules (Prospero, R3, Rh4) can be detected.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from expression analyses.

claim: R8 cells interact with Dm8 neurons most likely via ubiquitously expressed molecules such as N-Cadherin expressed in both R7 and R8 cells.
source: Thus, the R8 cells interact with Dm8 neurons most likely via ubiquitously expressed molecules such as N-Cadherin expressed in both, R7 as well as R8, cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of cell-type specific molecule changes and the GRASP data.

claim: N-Cadherin is required for stabilization of R8 axons at the layer M6.
source: This is supported by our observation that N-Cadherin is required for stabilization of R8 axons at the layer M6 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E–F').
evidence: The claim is supported by N-Cadherin mutant analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2F'.

claim: R8 axons form functional synapses with Dm8, a known R7 target neuron, in the layer M6.
source: We observed that R8 axons form functional synapses with Dm8, a known R7 target neuron, in the layer M6.
evidence: This is a summary of the GRASP experiments.

claim: Within M6, R7 axons form synapses with Dm8 but not with Tm5c which also arborize the M6 layer.
source: In fact, it has been shown that within M6, R7 axons form synapses with Dm8 but not with Tm5c (Karuppudurai et al., 2014) which also arborize the M6 layer.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Karuppudurai et al., 2014.

claim: Within layer M3, R8 and L3 select distinct post-synaptic partners.
source: Similarly in layer M3 R8 and L3 select distinct post-synaptic partners (Takemura et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Takemura et al., 2013.

claim: Medulla neurons are generated in temporal fashion.
source: Based on the data from Hasegawa et al., 2011; Li et al., 2013; Suzuki et al., 2013, the medulla neurons are generated in temporal fashion (reviewed in Sato et al., 2013; Suzuki and Sato, 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Medulla neurons likely innervate the medulla at different time points due to their temporal generation.
source: and therefore they likely innervate the medulla at different time points.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal generation of medulla neurons.

claim: The medulla context for arriving R cell axons reduces the complexity of synaptic partner selection.
source: Experiments presented here support a developmental scenario in which the medulla context for arriving R cell axons reduces the complexity of synaptic partner selection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: R8 and L3 have different arrival times at M3.
source: For example R8 and L3 have different arrival times at M3 (Nern et al., 2005; Pecot et al., 2013; 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations.

claim: R8 and L3 would encounter a different local environment of potential post-synaptic partners competent for synaptogenesis due to different arrival times.
source: thereby would encounter a different local environment of potential post-synaptic partners competent for synaptogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the different arrival times of R8 and L3.

claim: Some form of temporal co-ordination of afferent axons and their post-synaptic partner cell neurites would simplify the synaptic partner matching.
source: It is plausible that some form of temporal co-ordination of afferent axons and their post-synaptic partner cell neurites would actually simplify the synaptic partner matching.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the temporal coordination concept.

claim: R7 and R8 axons arriving at the same medulla position approximately the same time will pick the same synaptic partners exemplified by Dm8.
source: The concept of temporal identity would argue that R7 and R8 axons arriving at the same medulla position approximately the same time, as shown in the Sequoia gain-of-function background, will pick the same synaptic partners exemplified by Dm8.
evidence: This is inferred from the GRASP experiments showing R8->Dm8 contacts when R8 is mis-positioned.

claim: Proximity-based axon-target interaction for synaptogenesis is supported by earlier analysis of ectopic axons in Drosophila as well as Zebrafish.
source: Support for such proximity-based axon-target interaction for synaptogenesis comes from earlier analysis of ectopic axons in Drosophila as well as Zebrafish (Edwards and Meinertzhagen, 2009; Berger-Müller et al., 2013; Pujol-Martí et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: R7 is the most recently added cell to the precursor ommatidium from an evolutionary perspective.
source: From an evolutionary perspective, such proximity-induced synapse formation has several advantages over mechanisms that require regulation and expression of distinct sets of cell recognition molecules. Considering R7 as the most recently added cell to the precursor ommatidium (Mavromatakis and Tomlinson, 2012):
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mavromatakis and Tomlinson, 2012.

claim: During development, R7 is recruited using mechanisms similar to R8 and therefore possesses default R8 specification program.
source: During development, R7 is recruited using mechanisms similar to R8 and therefore possesses default R8 specification program.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about R7 development.

claim: The default R8 program is suppressed to facilitate R7 specification.
source: However, this default R8 program is suppressed to facilitate R7 specification (Cook et al., 2003; Morey et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cook et al., 2003 and Morey et al., 2008.

claim: A temporally separated, novel R7 cell is generated with basic neuronal differentiation similar to that of an R8 cell.
source: Thus, a temporally separated, novel R7 cell is generated with basic neuronal differentiation similar to that of an R8 cell (Brennan and Moses, 2000; Friedrich et al., 2011; Roignant and Treisman, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations.

claim: The temporal difference in the R8/R7 differentiation is translated into Sequoia mediated layer segregation of their growth cones.
source: Interestingly the temporal difference in the R8/R7 differentiation is then translated into Sequoia mediated layer segregation of their growth cones (Petrovic and Hummel, 2008), with Sequoia expression being part of common differentiation program.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Petrovic and Hummel, 2008 and the data in this study.

claim: The evolutionary recent R7 cell seems to recognize its synaptic targets via pan neuronal molecules like N-Cadherin as part of the default neuronal differentiation program, instead of the invention of an additional recognition code.
source: Thus, the evolutionary recent R7 cell seems to recognize its synaptic targets via pan neuronal molecules like N-Cadherin as part of the default neuronal differentiation program, instead of the invention of an additional recognition code.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the evolutionary perspective and the experimental data.
